markers.label: Tbilisi
markers.description: Georgia's post-Soviet government was already weakened by internal conflict and legitimacy problems.

markers.label: Sukhumi
markers.description: Sukhumi was the political prize and the capital of Abkhazia.

slides.title: A Separatist Crisis Inside a Georgian Crisis
slides.cap: Visual reference for Origins and Road to War.
slides.body: The War in Abkhazia began as Georgia tried to assert authority in a region where Abkhaz separatists feared domination by Tbilisi. The conflict overlapped with Georgia's own civil turmoil, Russian influence, North Caucasian volunteers, and competing memories of autonomy and demographic change.

stats.lbl: Abkhazia was not an isolated separatist fight; it unfolded while the Georgian state itself was fragile.

markers.label: Sukhumi
markers.description: Georgian forces entered the capital early in the war, shifting the crisis into full armed conflict.

markers.label: Abkhaz government retreat route
markers.description: Abkhaz separatist leaders retreated toward Gudauta, where Russian military presence mattered.

slides.title: A Quick Entry With Long Consequences
slides.cap: Visual reference for Georgian Entry into Sukhumi.
slides.body: Georgian forces entered Abkhazia claiming to secure rail lines and free officials, but the move became the start of a full war. Georgian control of Sukhumi did not settle the conflict; it radicalized Abkhaz resistance and pulled in outside fighters and Russian military influence.

stats.lbl: The opening operation achieved quick territorial control but helped create a wider coalition against Georgia.

title: Battle of Gagra
sub: A ceasefire collapses on the northwest coast

markers.label: Gagra
markers.description: The Abkhaz-led capture of Gagra reopened the war after a Moscow ceasefire.

markers.label: Russian border approach
markers.description: The northwest coast connected Abkhaz forces to North Caucasian volunteers and Russian-side logistics.

slides.title: The War Turns at Gagra
slides.cap: Visual reference for Battle of Gagra.
slides.body: After a ceasefire, Abkhaz forces and North Caucasian volunteers attacked Gagra. The fall of the town changed the war's momentum and was followed by violence against Georgian civilians. Gagra showed that ceasefire lines could collapse quickly when outside support and local revenge converged.

stats.lbl: Gagra shifted momentum away from Georgia and showed how the war's coastal geography linked Abkhazia to outside fighters.

title: Siege of Tkvarcheli
sub: An isolated town becomes a humanitarian and military symbol

markers.label: Tkvarcheli
markers.description: The besieged town became a symbol of Abkhaz endurance and outside humanitarian airlift.

markers.label: Eastern Abkhazia
markers.description: The east mattered because it connected Abkhazia's war to the Georgian-populated Gali and Ochamchire areas.

slides.title: The Besieged Mining Town
slides.body: Tkvarcheli was isolated for much of the war and supplied partly by air. Its siege mattered militarily and symbolically: Abkhaz narratives emphasized survival under blockade, while Georgian narratives stressed the wider war and attacks on Georgian civilians elsewhere. The town became one of the conflict's competing memory sites.

stats.lbl: Tkvarcheli shows how the war was fought through isolation, supply, airlift, and competing humanitarian narratives.

title: Gumista and March Offensive
sub: The northern approaches to Sukhumi become decisive

markers.label: Gumista River
markers.description: The Gumista line was the defensive barrier north of Sukhumi.

markers.label: Achadara-Kamani-Shroma area
markers.description: Villages north and east of Sukhumi became routes for pressure on the capital.

slides.title: The River Line Before Sukhumi
slides.body: The Gumista front was central because whoever broke it could threaten Sukhumi directly. Abkhaz and allied forces repeatedly tested Georgian defenses, while Georgian troops tried to hold the capital's northern shield. The fighting made the geography around Sukhumi as important as the city itself.

stats.lbl: The road to Sukhumi ran through villages, river crossings, and ridgelines that made the capital vulnerable.

title: Battle of Ochamchire
sub: The eastern front threatens Georgian-held territory

markers.label: Ochamchire
markers.description: Fighting around Ochamchire connected the eastern front to the wider collapse of Georgian positions.

markers.label: Gali district
markers.description: Gali's Georgian population later became central to displacement and return questions.

slides.title: Pressure in the East
slides.cap: Visual reference for Battle of Ochamchire.
slides.body: Fighting around Ochamchire and eastern Abkhazia widened pressure on Georgian positions and threatened routes toward Gali. The eastern front mattered because it linked battlefield movement to the fate of Georgian civilians in districts that would later be emptied or transformed by displacement.

stats.lbl: The eastern battles connected military pressure to the later geography of displacement.

title: Fall of Sukhumi
sub: The capital falls after the ceasefire breaks

markers.label: Sukhumi
markers.description: The fall of Sukhumi ended Georgian control over Abkhazia's capital.

markers.label: Supreme Soviet building
markers.description: The damaged parliament building became one of the war's most recognizable images.

slides.title: The Capital Falls
slides.cap: Visual reference for Fall of Sukhumi.
slides.body: Sukhumi fell in September 1993 after Abkhaz and allied forces broke through. Georgian leaders and civilians fled, and members of the Abkhaz government-in-exile were killed. The fall of Sukhumi decided the war militarily and opened the worst phase of ethnic cleansing against Georgians.

stats.lbl: The fall of the capital transformed Abkhazia from a contested war zone into a de facto separatist entity.

title: Ethnic Cleansing of Georgians
sub: Mass flight and violence reshape Abkhazia

markers.label: Sukhumi
markers.description: Violence after the fall of Sukhumi became central to Georgian memory of the war.

markers.label: Gali return corridor
markers.description: Gali later became the main district associated with partial Georgian return and continuing insecurity.

slides.title: A War That Remade the Population
slides.cap: Visual reference for Ethnic Cleansing of Georgians.
slides.body: After Georgian defeat, large numbers of ethnic Georgians fled or were expelled from Abkhazia. Killings, looting, and fear remade the region's demography. The human legacy of the war is inseparable from displacement: Abkhazia became de facto independent, but at the cost of a massive refugee and return problem.

stats.lbl: The war's outcome was not only territorial; it changed who could live safely in Abkhazia.

title: Outcome and Legacy
sub: De facto separation and unresolved return

markers.label: Sukhumi
markers.description: Sukhumi remained the de facto capital of separatist Abkhazia.

markers.label: Tbilisi
markers.description: Georgia continued to claim Abkhazia and treat displacement as a central national wound.

slides.title: Victory Without Recognition
slides.cap: Visual reference for Outcome and Legacy.
slides.body: Abkhaz forces won the war and established de facto separation from Georgia. International recognition did not follow, and the unresolved status of Abkhazia became one of the central post-Soviet conflicts. The legacy includes Russian leverage, Georgian displacement, and a frozen political settlement that later shaped the 2008 war.

stats.lbl: The unresolved Abkhazia conflict became part of the security architecture that led into later Georgian-Russian confrontation.
